weekly_ai_summary.policy_summary: 米国のワクチン政策に関する最新の報告では、がんワクチンの進展やインフルエンザワクチン研究の結果が示されています。また、COVIDワクチンの迅速かつ公平な配布が2022年までに数百万の死亡を防げた可能性があるとの政策提言もあります。
weekly_ai_summary.academic_summary: インドにおける健康な成人を対象とした研究で、カンボジアパスツール研究所とタイ赤十字社の皮内狂犬病ワクチンの免疫原性と安全性が評価されました。また、米国の退役軍人に対するmRNA-1345ワクチンの呼吸器合胞体ウイルスに対する有効性が検討されています。

The findings support the further development of affordable, easily administered mucosal vaccines that could improve access to immunisati
items.article_text_original: New MHRA research puts needle-free Strep A vaccine within reach Pioneering study by MHRA scientists advances innovative approach to vaccination and promise of vaccine against Strep A. New research by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in partnership with the GSK Vaccines Institute for Global Health, has moved a vaccine against the highly contagious group A streptococcus bacterium (Strep A) a step closer to reality. Published this month (October 2026), the paper, published in Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics, also shows promise for ‘needle-free’ vaccines which could be administered in the nose or under the tongue. There is currently no licensed vaccine for Strep A, despite it causing hundreds of millions of infections globally. Although most Strep infections are mild, serious complications can lead to long-term disability or death, particularly in low-and middle-income countries where the burden of the disease remains high. It is estimated that there are over 600 million Strep A infections worldwide each year with associated complications responsible for over 500,000 deaths. Dr Fatme Mawas, Head of Conjugate Vaccines, MHRA said: “This research highlights the potential of GMMA technology to support a new generation of affordable, needle-free vaccines. By delivering a Strep A vaccine through the nose or under the tongue, we showed that strong immune responses were generated both at the mucosal surfaces where infection begins and throughout the body, supporting protection against invasive disease. “This approach could make vaccines easier to administer and more accessible globally, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where the burden of Strep A disease is greatest. By preventing infections before they occur, vaccines can also help reduce antibiotic use and support efforts to tackle antimicrobial resistance.” The vaccine uses Generalised Modules for Membrane Antigens (GMMA) which are tiny bubbles naturally shed from bacteria, as both a carrier for the Strep A carbohydrate and an adjuvant to boost the immune response. Unlike most vaccine approaches, which focus primarily on generating antibodies in the bloodstream, this research targets immunity at mucosal surfaces of the nose and throat, where Strep A establishes infection, while also inducing broader systemic immune response. The findings support the further development of affordable, easily administered mucosal vaccines that could improve access to immunisation worldwide and contribute to global efforts to reduce the burden of infectious disease and antimicrobial resistance This work was conducted in a mouse (pre-clinical) model and forms part of the MHRA’s wider programme of research into vaccine science, immunology, assay development and novel vaccine delivery technologies. Notes to editors - The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is responsible for regulating all medicines and medical devices in the UK by ensuring they work and are acceptably safe. All our work is underpinned by robust and fact-based judgements to ensure that the benefits justify any risks. - The MHRA is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care. - For media enquiries, please contact the newscentre@mhra.gov.uk, or call on 020 3080 7651.

items.article_text_original: PAHO urges countries to close immunization gaps and strengthen surveillance to protect the Region from imported poliovirus Washington, D.C., 23 October 2026 (PAHO) – The Americas mark 35 years without a case of polio caused by wild poliovirus this World Polio Day, but vaccination coverage remains below the 95% target recommended by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), leaving the Region vulnerable to the reintroduction of the virus. In 2025, vaccination coverage continued to recover from declines during the COVID-19 pandemic, but remained below the recommended target for all three doses of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV). Some 91% of children received their first dose, up from 86% in 2024; 89% received their second dose, compared with 87% the previous year; and 87% received their third dose, up from 85% in 2024 and 80% in 2021. “The elimination of wild poliovirus from the Americas is one of the Region’s greatest public health achievements, but we cannot take it for granted,” said PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa. “As long as poliovirus circulates elsewhere, the risk of importation remains. Maintaining high vaccination coverage and strong surveillance is essential to protect children and prevent the virus from regaining a foothold.” In 1975, nearly 6,000 polio cases were reported in the Americas. The last case of wild poliovirus in the Americas was recorded on 23 August 1991 in Peru, in an unvaccinated two-year-old child who developed irreversible paralysis. In 1994, the Americas became the first region in the world to be certified free of wild poliovirus transmission. This achievement followed decades of sustained immunization efforts across the Region, supported by strong surveillance and cooperation among countries. Mass vaccination campaigns and expanded access to routine immunization helped interrupt transmission, demonstrating the impact of coordinated public health action. Detecting and preventing imported cases Although the Region has been free of wild poliovirus for 35 years, the virus could still be imported from countries where it continues to circulate. In communities with low vaccination coverage, it could spread and cause outbreaks. Today, endemic transmission of wild poliovirus continues in Afghanistan and Pakistan. According to the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), 48 cases of wild poliovirus had been reported globally in 2026 as of 20 October, 42 in Afghanistan and six in Pakistan. The Region’s ability to detect possible polio cases quickly also needs strengthening. Health authorities monitor cases of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP), a sudden loss of muscle strength that can have many causes but is also a key warning sign for polio. Each case is investigated to rule out poliovirus. Over the past year, countries in the Americas reported 0.85 AFP cases per 100,000 children under 15, below the surveillance target of at least 1 case per 100,000. Reaching this target helps demonstrate that surveillance systems are sensitive enough to detect and investigate potential cases of polio. Polio is a highly contagious disease that mainly affects children under five. The virus can invade the nervous system and cause irreversible paralysis within days. Among those who develop paralysis, 5%–10% die when their breathing muscles become immobilized. There is no cure, but vaccination can prevent the disease. A global effort that must continue The Americas’ achievement is part of a global effort to eradicate polio. In 1988, the World Health Assembly launched the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), when an estimated 350,000 children were paralyzed by the disease each year in more than 125 countries. Since then, polio cases have fallen by 99.9%. An estimated 20 million people are walking today who would otherwise have been paralyzed, and more than 1.5 million lives have been saved. These gains demonstrate what sustained vaccination and international cooperation can achieve. But as long as poliovirus transmission continues anywhere in the world, every country remains at risk. Without eradication, polio could resurge and cause up to 200,000 new cases annually within a decade, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Protecting the Americas’ achievement PAHO works with countries to strengthen routine immunization, improve surveillance and ensure health systems can rapidly detect and respond to suspected polio cases. Maintaining high and equitable vaccination coverage is essential to prevent imported poliovirus from spreading and to protect the Region’s polio-free status. On World Polio Day, October 24, PAHO urges parents and caregivers to check that children are up to date with their polio vaccinations and to complete any missed doses. Ensuring every child receives the recommended vaccines will help protect the Americas’ achievement and bring the world closer to eradicating polio.
